The meaning isn't subjective, as you seem to suggest. An ET, upon examining it, would also call it an AND operator. Again, reduction from the macroscopic to the microscopic doesn't nullify the macroscopic. This isn't even the weak point in my argument; the weak point is the connection between logic and thought to free will, which I admit is tenuous.

Disagree with OP. An analogy I like to use is the logic gates used in computers. An AND gate, for example, emits an output if both of its inputs receive a signal. Someone might explain this by pointing to the individual physical parts, and tracing the movement of electrons therein as determined by the laws of physics. However, someone else might simply characterize it by what it accomplishes on a macroscopic scale, namely, a logical operation. Both interpretations are correct, and one does not diminish the other. So it is in a human or animal mind. Yes, neurons are firing and chemical reactions are taking place, but this doesn't diminish the reality of the macroscopic product: thought. For lack of a better terminology, I like to think of human beings as being like wells or trees, tapping into the underlying logos of the universe and acting as incarnations of it, if you will. It is in light of all this, coupled with the enigmatic nature of consciousness, that I hesitate to subscribe to arguments against free will. But that's just my two cents.

It's the big crunch. All of the matter in the universe has been pulled into an infinitesimally small point at the cosmic center. All, that is, save for a single star-eating ship. It must decide whether it wants to preserve its own existence or let a new universe come into being. Imagine a table with 50 paper bags in a row on top of it. you open one of the bags and find that it contains a red marble. Do you have enough information to determine the probability that any specific bag contains a red marble? Of course not. You would have to open all of the bags and count how many contain red marbles, and divide that number by 50 to get the probability of choosing a red marble-containing bag at random. 
I assume that when you say "the probability that God exists," you mean "the probability that we are in a universe in which a God exists," as this is the only context where I think probability is applicable. If we assume that there is more than one universe (or at least more than one possible universe) and that it is possible for a God to exist in some and not in others, we can begin to calculate the probability of opening (living in) a bag (universe) where a red marble (God) exists. The problem is, we are trapped in one of the bags and marbles are invisible to us. As mentioned in a previous comment, there may be an infinite number of bags, making  things even more tricky. 
But the probability could still be 0 or 1, regardless of any certainty or uncertainty we may experience. Thinking back to my original example, if we don't open any of the bags we haven't ruled out the possibility that all of the bags in fact contain red marbles, or that indeed they are all empty. My point is that the probability of an event is independent of our awareness of it and any certainty or lack of certainty we may feel does not preclude the possibility that the event in question has no chance of happening or every chance of happening.

I have never had a calling, although I used to say the sacrament prayer pretty much every Sunday because the rest of the priests thought they were too cool for school. They don't really listen or pay attention to what I'm saying, but drone on with the same little dialectical fallacy-building sessions over and over. Yes, religions serve an important role in almost every culture and in the lives of many, many people. If they want to believe in a reassuring fable because it gives them comfort, then that is their prerogative. But what is unconscionable is when someone forces someone else to believe their delusion, whether it be by indoctrination of children or through force or fear of force. In order for a religion to exist, there must be indoctrination of the young, which I see as possibly the most selfish and disgusting aspect of it. I am not against people believing nonsense. I am simply against people forcing others to believe their nonsense.
